stops.name: Angers, news from Caspe: the crown forfeited but the claim kept
stops.campa: Word reaches Angers from the assembly at Caspe: the nine electors of Aragon, weighing the rival claims after Martín's death without heir, have passed over Louis III, Yolande's own son, her father's grandson, in favor of the Castilian prince Fernando de Antequera. The Angevin claim to Aragon is dead in law. Yolande does not surrender it in fact. She and her children go on styling themselves kings and queens of Aragon for the rest of their lives, a paper crown worn over the real work of winning an entirely different kingdom.

stops.name: Paris, the Cabochien mob: the Burgundian match broken
stops.campa: In Paris a Cabochien mob loyal to John the Fearless of Burgundy bursts into the dauphin's own palace and seizes him under his mother's eyes. Yolande reads the violence correctly: she and Louis repudiate at once the engagement of their son to Burgundy's own daughter Catherine, breaking cleanly with the duke who has just shown what he does with princes in his power. The house of Anjou declares itself, irreversibly, for the Armagnac cause and for the sickly third son of the king whom nobody yet imagines will be worth the wager.

stops.name: Paris, the betrothal of Marie and Charles sealed
stops.campa: In Paris, under Queen Isabeau's own auspices, Yolande presents her children and finalizes the marriage contract binding her daughter Marie to Charles, the queen's third surviving son, a boy nobody expects to reign, offered almost as an afterthought once his mother has already promised his sister Catherine to Burgundy. Yolande sees past the afterthought. She takes the engagement as the opening she has been maneuvering toward since the Cabochien riots, and begins at once arranging to take the boy out of Paris and into her own household.

stops.name: Angers, the dauphin brought north, out of the Burgundians' reach
stops.campa: At the beginning of the year Yolande brings the ten-year-old Charles and her own daughter Marie out of Paris and into her duchies of Anjou and Provence, away from both the Burgundians circling the mad king's court and Isabeau's own erratic favor. She raises the boy as her own from this point on, feeding him, tutoring him, surrounding him with her own captains and counselors, building, without yet naming it, the court-in-exile from which a broken kingdom will eventually be rebuilt.

stops.name: Angers, birth of Charles, Count of Maine
stops.campa: A last son, Charles, is born at Angers, the fifth and youngest of Yolande's children, who will grow up alongside his foster-brother the dauphin more nearly than his own elder brothers, close enough in age and household that the two boys are effectively raised as a single generation of princes. Charles of Anjou will stand at his mother's side in the palace intrigues of the 1430s, one more piece she has placed years in advance for a game not yet declared.

stops.name: Angers, death of Louis II: the sole regency begins
stops.campa: Louis II dies at Angers, worn down by years of Italian campaigning that won him battles and no kingdom. Yolande, thirty-three years old, becomes at a stroke sole regent of Anjou, Provence and Maine for her thirteen-year-old heir Louis III, and, in practice, guardian of a second heir who is not even her own son by blood: Charles, made dauphin of France this same spring by the death of his own elder brother Jean. Two boys, two duchies, one widow now running both.

stops.name: Angers, "we have not nurtured this one," the refusal to Isabeau
stops.campa: Queen Isabeau, allied now with Burgundy and estranged from her own surviving son, sends to Angers demanding the dauphin be returned to the royal court in Paris. Yolande's answer, kept by the Angevin chronicler Bourdigné, becomes the sentence her whole widowhood turns on: she has not raised this boy to watch him die like his brothers, go mad like his father, or turn English like his mother. She will keep him for her own. Isabeau may come and take him, she says, if she dares. No one comes.
stops.quote: We have not nurtured and cherished this one for you to make him die like his brothers or to go mad like his father, or to become English like you. I keep him for my own. Come and take him away, if you dare.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Yolande of Aragon by the Angevin chronicler Jehan de Bourdigné, Chronique d'Anjou et du Maine (16th c.); cited in Rohr, Yolande of Aragon, and standard biographies

stops.name: Bar-le-Duc, Cardinal Louis of Bar adopts René as heir
stops.campa: In Lorraine, Cardinal Louis, aged duke of Bar and great-uncle to Yolande's second son, formally adopts the ten-year-old René as heir to his county: the same county of Bar whose thirteenth- and fourteenth-century counts once held the Bourlémont lords of Domrémy in liege homage, the same overlordship recorded in the 1334 aveu that binds the forte maison of Domrémy to Bar rather than to Lorraine or France outright. Yolande's blood runs to Bar twice over now: her own mother born of its house, and her son about to rule it.

stops.name: Angers, the prophecy kept current: Marie Robine's armed virgin
stops.campa: At her own court Yolande keeps alive the prophecy the dying recluse Marie Robine of Avignon left behind at the turn of the century: that France, ruined by a woman, would be saved by an armed virgin sent from the marches of the kingdom, a saying already fused in the countryside of Lorraine with the older word of Merlin about a maid out of the Bois Chenu. Yolande's own network of clergy and informants keeps the saying current in exactly the households closest to Domrémy, so that when a girl finally comes claiming the mantle, the court already knows the words to test her by.

stops.name: Chinon, Richemont made Constable of France
stops.campa: At Chinon, the castle that will in four years host the audience of her life's greatest discovery, Yolande secures the appointment of Arthur de Richemont, brother of the Duke of Brittany, as Constable of France, pulling Brittany decisively out of the English orbit and giving the dauphin's threadbare cause its first real soldier of rank. It is a marriage-broker's move dressed as a military appointment: Richemont will marry into the Burgundian family and fight against it anyway, bound now to Yolande's Angevin faction by an office only the crown, meaning in practice Yolande, can grant.

stops.name: Chinon, the audience secured
stops.campa: A girl out of Domrémy, in the Bar country whose overlordship Yolande's own son now holds, has reached Chinon claiming voices and a mission. It is Yolande's household and Yolande's faction, La Trémoille notwithstanding, that clears the way for the audience the council has debated for two days: torchlight, three hundred knights, a decoy dauphin, and Charles found out anyway in the crowd. Yolande has spent sixteen years building exactly the court that would recognize, rather than burn, a claim like this one. Tonight it does not burn her.

stops.name: Poitiers, the matrons' examination
stops.campa: While the doctors of the University turn the Maid's words over for three weeks at Poitiers, Yolande takes charge of the other examination that matters as much to the court as theology: whether the girl is in fact a virgin, and so not a witch working through carnal commerce with the Devil. Yolande and her chosen matrons examine Jehanne themselves and certify her intact, a verdict from the queen of Sicily's own household that closes the gate the Poitiers doctors could not close alone, the one that would otherwise deliver the Maid straight to a witchcraft charge.
